docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
KOR-ee, from the greek Κόρη, the queen of the underworld, daughter of Zeus and Demeter. Kore is a numerical tool to study the core flow within rapidly rotating planets or other rotating fluids contained within near-spherical boundaries. The current version solves the linear Navier-Stokes and induction equations for a viscous, incompressible and conductive fluid with an externally imposed magnetic field, and enclosed within a rotating spherical shell.

Kore assumes all dynamical variables to oscillate in a harmonic fashion. The oscillation frequency can be imposed externally, as is the case when doing forced motion studies (e.g. tidal forcing), or it can be obtained as part of the solution to an eigenvalue problem. In Kore's current implementation, the eigenmodes are the inertial modes of the rotating fluid. Inertial modes are the global modes of a rotating flow in which the Coriolis force participates prominently in the restoring force balance.

Kore's distinctive feature is the use of a very efficient spectral method employing Gegenbauer (also known as ultraspherical) polynomials as a basis in the radial direction. This approach leads to sparse matrices representing the differential equations, as opposed to dense matrices, as in traditional Chebyshev colocation methods. Sparse matrices have smaller memory-footprint and are more suitable for systematic core flow studies at extremely low viscosities (or small Ekman numbers).

Kore is free for everyone to use, with no restrictions. Too often in the scientific literature the numerical methods used are presented with enough detail to guarantee reproducibility, but only in principle. Without access to the actual implementation of those methods, which would require a significant amount of work and time to develop, readers are left effectively without the possibility to reproduce or verify the results presented. This leads to very slow scientific progress. We share our code to avoid this.

If this code is useful for your research, we invite you to cite the relevant papers (coming soon) and hope that you can also contribute to the project.

docs.title: Background model
docs.text:
kore solves for small perturbations of a background in which the density \(\rho_0\), the pressure (or \(p_0 = \rho_0 T_0\)) and gravity \(g\) depend on \(r\) only, the entropy has a radial gradient \(dS/dr\), and the viscosity \(\nu\) and the thermal diffusivity \(\kappa\) are radial profiles. The background has three parts, each chosen by name in the parameter file:

part parameter what it sets structure structure \(\rho_0\), \(p_0\) and \(g\) stratification stratification \(dS/dr\), with \(S = \delta s/c_p\) (only with thermal = 1) diffusivity diffusivity the radial profiles of \(\nu\) and \(\kappa\)

The rotation of the background, uniform or differential, is chosen separately (differential-rotation.md). The code is in bin/background.py (the choice, the checks, the stratification and diffusivity types) and bin/radial_profiles.py (one class per structure). These names replaced model_type, heating, solar_rz, solar_density and aux0 on 2026-10-26; the last section translates old parameter files.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
kore is dimensionless. The unit of length is the radius of the outer wall, \(r = 1\). r_out is that radius in star radii (1 by default), so \(x = r\cdot\)r_out is the radius in star radii. With Gaspard = 1 the unit of time is \(1/\Omega\); then ViscosD \(= \nu/(\Omega L^2)\), ThermaD \(= \kappa/(\Omega L^2)\) with \(L\) = r_out star radii, and the buoyancy frequency is

\[ N^2 = \mathrm{Beyonce}\thinspace g\thinspace \frac{dS}{dr} \]

in units of \(\Omega^2\). The only physical unit kore reads is that of the solar rotation data, in nHz.

bin/units.py converts physical values; kore itself never imports it. In a parameter file, after r_out is set:

import units
units.set_physical(par, frame_nHz=456.0, nu=1e12, kappa=1e12)   # Gaspard, Beyonce, ViscosD, ThermaD, diff_rot_frame
units.set_target(par, omega=-271.2, sigma=-33.2)                 # itau, rtau from ω, σ in nHz

set_physical takes \(\nu\) and \(\kappa\) in cm²/s, and the solar radius and surface gravity unless radius and gsurf (cgs) are given; Beyonce \(= g_{\rm surf}/(L\Omega^2)\) assumes \(g = 1\) at the surface, as in the solar structures. In a run directory, python3 bin/units.py prints the eigenvalues as \(\omega\) and \(\sigma\) in nHz in the rotating frame.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
The background of the smooth Sun example (examples/smooth_sun/parameters.py):

par.thermal        = 1
par.r_out          = 0.985                 # outer wall in solar radii
par.structure      = 'model S hydrostatic'
par.stratification = 'solar_rz'            # a radiative interior below a slightly subadiabatic convection zone
par.solar_rz_delta_cz = -4e-7
par.diffusivity    = 'solar_rz'            # ν, κ drop to visc0, therm0 below 0.70 R☉
par.visc0, par.therm0 = 0.01, 0.04
units.set_physical(par, frame_nHz=456.0, nu=1e12, kappa=1e12)

The checked-in bin/parameters.py, a gravito-inertial mode, uses structure = 'Wu 2005' with r_out = 0.99 and stratification = 'top hat'.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:

  • Only ratios of \(\rho_0\) and of \(p_0\) enter the equations, so their scale does not matter. \(g\) is 1 at the surface (\(x = 1\)) in the solar structures and in 'Wu 2005'.
  • The three solar structures (the first and the last two rows) also make \(x = r\cdot\)r_out the radius of the solar rotation profiles (diff_rot.solar_x).
  • 'model S hydrostatic' is within 1.0 %, 0.5 % and 0.75 % of Model S in \(\rho\), \(p\) and \(g\) at degree 30, and within 0.14 %, 0.06 % and 0.10 % at degree 50. Use 50 to compare with papers that use Model S itself; degrees of 40 and above need about 16 more lmax for the same \(\ell\)-convergence of the HFR modes (heat-equation.md §8, "Hydrostatic structure").
  • The two legacy structures are kept so that runs made before 'model S hydrostatic' give the same results. For 'old model S prototype', solar_density_window None fits the shell \([\)ricb\(\cdot\)r_out \(- 0.01\), r_out \(+ 0.005]\) when ricb > 0, and is 'sun' when ricb = 0: one even fit over the whole Sun of degree solar_density_sun_deg (60) (heat-equation.md §8, "Model S density").

docs.title: Stratification
docs.text:
With thermal = 1, stratification sets \(dS/dr\) for \(r \ge 0\), in units of \(1/L\); it has no default then. In a full sphere (ricb = 0) kore uses it as an odd function of \(r\), so it should go to zero smoothly at the centre.

stratification \(dS/dr\) parameters 'top hat' \(\tfrac{A}{2}\left[\mathrm{erf}\frac{r - x_1}{w_1} - \mathrm{erf}\frac{r - x_2}{w_2}\right]\) aux1…aux5 = \(x_1\), \(w_1\), \(x_2\), \(w_2\), \(A\) 'odd top hat' the same made odd in \(r\): with \(x_1 = 0\) it rises as \(A\thinspace\mathrm{erf}(r/w_1)\) from the centre aux1…aux5 'solar_rz' the radiative interior of Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025b, below solar_rz_dSdr, solar_rz_steps, solar_rz_core, solar_rz_delta_cz, solar_rz_delta_sf, solar_rz_os 'linear' \(r\); with 'uniform', \(N^2\) = Beyonce \(r^2\) (Rieutord 2006, Mirouh et al. 2016) – 'inverse square' \(1/r^2\), conduction between the walls needs ricb > 0 'user' stratification_profile, a numpy expression (below) stratification_param (\(p\))
  • 'top hat' in a full sphere needs \(x_1 \gtrsim 6 w_1\), so that \(dS/dr \to 0\) at the centre; otherwise use 'odd top hat'. With ricb > 0 and ThermaD = 0, a \(dS/dr \neq 0\) at the inner wall gives spurious modes trapped there.
  • 'odd top hat' with aux1…aux5 = 0, 0.03, 0.68, 0.06, 2.6 fits the \(dS/dr\) of Model S to 10 % rms.

'solar_rz'. With \(x = r\cdot\)r_out in solar radii (their eq. 10, plus the convection zone of Bekki et al. 2024, eq. 2):

\[ \frac{dS}{dr} = \frac{A}{4}\left[1 - \mathrm{erf}\frac{x - x_1}{d}\right]\left[1 - \mathrm{erf}\frac{x - x_2}{d}\right]\mathrm{erf}\frac{x}{w_0} + \delta(x)\thinspace \frac{d\ln p_0}{dr}\thinspace \frac{1}{2}\left[1 + \mathrm{erf}\frac{x - x_{OS}}{d_{OS}}\right], \] \[ \delta(x) = \delta_{cz} + (\delta_{sf} - \delta_{cz})\thinspace e^{-((x - 0.985)/0.015)^2}, \]

with \(A\) = solar_rz_dSdr (2.615), \([x_1, x_2, d]\) = solar_rz_steps ([0.61, 0.68, 0.04]), \(w_0\) = solar_rz_core (0.05: makes \(dS/dr\) odd and smooth at \(r = 0\), no effect above \(x \approx 3w_0\)), \([x_{OS}, d_{OS}]\) = solar_rz_os ([0.70, 0.04]) and \(\delta_{cz}\), \(\delta_{sf}\) = solar_rz_delta_cz, solar_rz_delta_sf (0). \(A\) is their \((\partial s_0/\partial r)_{RZ}\) = 1.32e-2 erg g⁻¹ K⁻¹ cm⁻¹ times \(L/c_p\), with \(c_p\) = 3.46e8 and r_out = 0.985, so it scales with r_out. \(\delta < 0\) is subadiabatic; kore stops if \(\delta\) is set with another stratification. The fits of \(\delta_{cz}\) to the observed HFR frequencies are in heat-equation.md §8.

docs.title: Diffusivity
docs.text:
\( u\) = ViscosD \(\hat u(r)\) and \(\kappa\) = ThermaD \(\hat\kappa(r)\); diffusivity sets \(\hat u\) and \(\hat\kappa\).

diffusivity \(\hat u\), \(\hat\kappa\) parameters 'uniform' (default) 1 – 'step' visc0, therm0 below \(r\) = aux3, 1 above, joined by an erf of width aux4 visc0, therm0, aux3, aux4 'solar_rz' visc0, therm0 below \(x_{OS}\), 1 above, as \( frac12[1 + \mathrm{erf}((x - x_{OS})/d_{OS})]\) (Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025b, eqs. 8–9) visc0, therm0, solar_rz_os 'user' diffusivity_profiles = {'nu': '...', 'kappa': '...'}, numpy expressions (below) diffusivity_param (\(p\))
  • With 'step' and 'solar_rz', ViscosD and ThermaD are the values above the step (the convection zone of the Sun). Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025b use visc0 = 0.01 and therm0 = 0.04.
  • Any type is multiplied by \(( ho_0(x_2)/ ho_0)^p\), \(x_2\) = aux3, with \(p\) = visc_pow for \(\hat u\) and therm_pow for \(\hat\kappa\): 0 (the default) keeps the kinematic diffusivities as set, 1 makes \( ho_0 u\) and \( ho_0\kappa\) follow the profile instead.
  • Forcing 11 (random Reynolds stresses) uses the turbulent part of the viscosity, ViscosD \((\hat u - u_f)\): the floor \( u_f\) is visc0 with 'step' and 'solar_rz' when visc0 < 1 and 0 otherwise, unless rsf_nu_floor is set.

docs.title: 'user' profiles
docs.text:
stratification_profile and the two diffusivity_profiles are numpy expressions of r (the kore radius), x (as in the rotation profiles: \(r\cdot\)r_out with a solar structure, \(r\) otherwise) and p, with the functions listed for diff_rot_profiles in differential-rotation.md (exp, tanh, erf, abs, where, …). For example:

par.stratification = 'user'
par.stratification_profile = '2.5*exp(-((r - 0.75)/0.06)**2)'      # dS/dr in 1/L for r >= 0
par.diffusivity = 'user'
par.diffusivity_profiles = {'nu': '0.01 + 0.99*0.5*(1 + tanh((x - 0.70)/0.015))', 'kappa': '1'}

kore evaluates them at \(\lvert r\rvert\), so in a full sphere \(dS/dr\) is odd and \(\hat\nu\), \(\hat\kappa\) are even whatever the expression; for a profile that is smooth at the centre, \(dS/dr\) should still vanish there. The expressions must not contain #: spin_doctor writes them at the end of each params.dat row, after a #.

docs.title: Checks and output
docs.text:
Before anything is built, kore stops on a background that cannot work: an unknown type, one of the former names below, 'Wu 2005' without \(0 <\) r_out \(< 1\), 'inverse square' with ricb = 0, \(\delta\) without 'solar_rz', or a 'user' expression that does not evaluate. submatrices.py also warns about any name in the parameter file that kore does not define, so a misspelt name is not ignored without notice.

spin_doctor writes the background to params.dat (the full list of columns is in differential-rotation.md, Output). The columns, counted from 1:

  • 19 r_out, 20–24 aux1…aux5, 25 visc0, 34 therm0, 35 visc_pow, 36 therm_pow;
  • 63 structure, as its index in background.STRUCTURES: '8-term fit' 0, 'old model S prototype' 1, 'model S hydrostatic' 2, 'Wu 2005' 3, 'uniform' 4;
  • 64 the degree of the Model S fit (structure_deg for 'model S hydrostatic'), 65–66 the window of the 'old model S prototype' fits (nan: the default; 'sun': ∓(r_out + 0.005)), 67 solar_rz (1 when the stratification is 'solar_rz'), 68–74 its parameters, 77–78 \(\delta_{cz}\), \(\delta_{sf}\);
  • 81 stratification and 82 diffusivity, as their index in background.STRATIFICATIONS ('top hat' 0, 'odd top hat' 1, 'solar_rz' 2, 'linear' 3, 'inverse square' 4, 'user' 5; −1 without a stratification) and background.DIFFUSIVITIES ('uniform' 0, 'step' 1, 'solar_rz' 2, 'user' 3);
  • the 'user' expressions, at the end of the row after a # that np.loadtxt skips (a row with nothing to note has no #).

Columns 1–80 have the positions they had before these names, so scripts that read params.dat by column keep working.

docs.title: Differential rotation
docs.text:
kore can compute the linear oscillation modes of a star or planet whose rotation rate varies with radius and latitude, not only of a rigidly rotating one. The background rotation is

\[ \Omega(r,\theta) = \Omega_{\rm ref}\left[1 + \Delta\Omega(r,\theta)\right], \qquad \Delta\Omega = \sum_n f_n(r)\thinspace P_n(\cos\theta), \quad n = 0, 2, 4, \dots \]

Here \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\) is the rotation rate of the frame in which kore solves, and \(\Delta\Omega\) is the relative departure from it, written as a sum of Legendre polynomials in \(\cos\theta\) with radial coefficients \(f_n(r)\). Only even \(n\) appear, so the rotation is symmetric about the equator.

This page is the user guide: what is modelled, the parameters, the built-in profiles and their limits, and two worked examples. The derivation and the implementation notes are in heat-equation.md (thermal terms, generic \(P_n\) couplings, benchmarks, and a table of notation and code names) and in thermad0.md (runs without thermal diffusion, ThermaD = 0). The checks are described in tests/diff_rot/README.md and tests/heat_dr/README.md.

docs.title: What is modelled
docs.text:
kore solves in a frame rotating at \(\Omega_{ m ref}\). In that frame the differential rotation is a steady azimuthal flow,

\[ \mathbf{U}_ 0 = G hinspace \Delta\Omega hinspace r\sin heta hinspace \hat{\mathbf{e}}_ \phi , \]

where \(G\) = Gaspard \(= \Omega_{ m ref} au\) is the frame's rotation rate in kore's time unit \( au\) (1 with timescale = 'rotation'). Gaspard only sets the time unit; the frame itself is fixed by the profile, since \(\Delta\Omega\) is measured relative to it (diff_rot_frame for the solar profiles). The perturbation \(\mathbf u\) is advected and sheared by this flow. In the momentum equation this adds

\[ G\left[\Delta\Omega hinspace (i hinspace m hinspace \mathbf{u} + 2\hat{\mathbf{z}} imes\mathbf{u}) + r\sin heta hinspace (\mathbf{u}\cdot abla\Delta\Omega) hinspace \hat{\mathbf{e}}_ \phi ight]. \]

The first part is the advection by the local rotation and its Coriolis force, the second the transport of angular momentum by the perturbation across the shear. The density stratification is carried through the anelastic form of the velocity,

\[ \mathbf{u} = ho_0^{-1} abla imes abla imes( ho_0 P hinspace \mathbf{r}) + abla imes(T hinspace \mathbf{r}), \]

with \(P\) and \(T\) the poloidal and toroidal scalars that kore solves for.

With thermal = 1 the entropy equation gains up to three terms,

\[ i hinspace m G hinspace \Delta\Omega hinspace s + u_r hinspace rac{\partial S_{tw}}{\partial r} + rac{u_ heta}{r} hinspace rac{\partial S_{tw}}{\partial heta}. \]

The first is the advection of the entropy perturbation \(s\) by \(\mathbf U_0\). The other two are the advection of a latitudinal background entropy \(S_{tw}(r, heta)\) by the perturbation. \(S_{tw}\) is either the thermal wind that balances \(\Omega(r, heta)\) (the latitudinal entropy a differentially rotating star needs to be in equilibrium; Bekki, Cameron & Gizon 2022, eq. 27) or prescribed. These thermal-wind terms are not small corrections: in a convection zone they act at the same order as the momentum terms (heat-equation.md §1).

Not modelled:

  • the background is fixed: nothing maintains or evolves \(\Omega\) and \(S_{tw}\) against diffusion;
  • \( ho_0\), \(T_0\) and \(g\) stay spherical (no centrifugal distortion);
  • there is no magnetic field.

Where it lives. Everything specific to the differential rotation (profiles, thermal wind, couplings, the terms of each row) is in bin/diff_rot.py, built on the angular algebra of bin/angular.py; the details are in differential_rotation_details.md. The rotation profiles do not depend on the background model (background.md).

docs.title: Frame and units
docs.text:
\(\Delta\Omega\) is relative to the frame, and \(G\) converts it to the time unit, so any timescale works. Two things follow:

  • ViscosD, ThermaD and Beyonce must be computed for \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\). For 'solar' the frame must rotate at 435 nHz; for 'solar_P4' and 'tabulated' at diff_rot_frame (456 nHz by default). The other types are dimensionless.
  • With thermal_wind = 2 the eigenvalues do not depend on the choice of frame. With thermal_wind = 1 (linear in \(\Delta\Omega\)) they do, at second order in \(\Delta\Omega\): 0.1–0.9 nHz for the solar modes of heat-equation.md §6.

Eigenvalues are in the rotating frame of \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\), as for uniform rotation.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
par.diff_rot           = 1
par.diff_rot_type      = 'conical'   # see the table of profiles below
par.diff_rot_ampl = -0.25            # the factor of ΔΩ: ε for 'conical'
par.thermal_wind       = 1           # only read with thermal = 1; needs Beyonce > 0

Then run submatrices.py, assemble.py and solve.py as usual. As for every run, lmax - m + 1 must be a multiple of 2*ncpus (assemble.py stops otherwise).

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
\(a\) = diff_rot_ampl, \(p\) = diff_rot_param. For the solar types \(x\) is the fractional solar radius: \(x = r\times\)r_out with a solar structure (background.md), \(x = r\) otherwise.

diff_rot_type \(\Delta\Omega(r,\theta)\) degrees notes 'rigid' \(a\) \(P_0\) test profile: a uniform offset of the rotation rate, with an exact answer (below); \(a = 0\) gives uniform rotation with the diff-rot machinery on (needed for thermal_wind = 3) 'Y20' \(a\thinspace P_2(\cos\theta)\) \(P_2\) \(P_2\) unnormalised, despite the name 'Y20-wall-bounded' \(a\thinspace (1 - r)(r - r_i)\thinspace P_2(\cos\theta)\), \(r_i\) = ricb \(P_2\) not smooth at \(r = 0\): use ricb > 0 'shellular' \(a\thinspace (r^\sigma - 1)\), \(\sigma = p\) \(P_0\) Baruteau & Rieutord 2013 (\(a = 1\)); not smooth at \(r = 0\) unless \(\sigma\) is even and positive 'shellular_boussinesq' \(\tfrac12 N_0^2\thinspace (1 - r^2)\), \(N_0^2 = a\) \(P_0\) Mirouh et al. 2016; use thermal_wind = 0 (their background has no thermal wind), structure 'uniform' and stratification 'linear' 'cylindrical' \(\varepsilon\thinspace r^2\sin^2\theta\), \(\varepsilon = a\) \(P_0\), \(P_2\) Baruteau & Rieutord 2013; barotropic, \(S_{tw} = 0\) 'conical' \(\varepsilon\sin^2\theta\), \(\varepsilon = a\) \(P_0\), \(P_2\) Guenel et al. 2016 'solar' \(a\thinspace \times\) helioseismic fit, \(P_0 + P_2\), tanh step at \(x = 0.71\) of width 0.1 \(P_0\), \(P_2\) relative to 435 nHz; 4.5 nHz too fast at the equator and 12 nHz at the pole compared with the observations (heat-equation.md §6) 'solar_P4' \(a\thinspace (\Omega/\Omega_{\rm ref} - 1)\), \(\Omega\) the fit below \(P_0\), \(P_2\), \(P_4\) diff_rot_solar, diff_rot_frame; defaults from Mukhopadhyay et al. 2026 'tabulated' \(a\thinspace (\Omega/\Omega_{\rm ref} - 1)\), \(\Omega\) from diff_rot_file \(P_0 \dots P_{n_{\max}}\) below 'user' \(a\sum_n f_n(r) P_n(\cos\theta)\), \(f_n\) from diff_rot_profiles the keys of diff_rot_profiles below

'rigid'. The eigenvalues are known exactly: with \(\lambda_0\) the diff_rot = 0 eigenvalue,

\[ \lambda(a, G) = \lambda_0\big(G(1 + a)\big) - i\thinspace m G a . \]

'solar_P4'. A rigid radiative zone joined by an erf step at the tachocline \(r_{tc}\) (width \(d_{tc}\)) to a convection zone whose rotation depends on latitude only:

\[ \frac{\Omega}{2\pi} = \Omega_{RZ} + \tfrac12\left[\Omega_{CZ}(\theta) - \Omega_{RZ}\right]\left[1 + \mathrm{erf}\thinspace \frac{x - r_{tc}}{d_{tc}}\right], \qquad \Omega_{CZ} = c_0 + c_2\cos^2\theta + c_4\cos^4\theta , \]

with diff_rot_solar = [\(c_0\), \(c_2\), \(c_4\), \(\Omega_{RZ}\), \(r_{tc}\), \(d_{tc}\)] (nHz, and fractions of R☉).

'user'. diff_rot_profiles gives the shape of each even degree as a numpy expression of r (kore radius), x (fractional solar radius) and p (diff_rot_param), with sin, cos, tan, arcsin, arccos, arctan, sinh, cosh, tanh, exp, log, log10, sqrt, abs, sign, pi, where, minimum, maximum, erf, erfc. For example, the cylindrical rotation as a 'user' profile (it gives the same matrices as 'cylindrical'):

par.diff_rot_type     = 'user'
par.diff_rot_profiles = {0: '(2/3)*r**2', 2: '-(2/3)*r**2'}
par.diff_rot_ampl     = -0.25

The degrees must be even, and the expressions must not contain #: spin_doctor writes them at the end of each params.dat row, after a #. Any degree up to 16 works with thermal_wind = 2 (32 with thermal_wind = 1).

'tabulated'. The file holds ome[θ, r] (nHz), r (R☉) and theta (rad), the layout of data/diff_rot.npz of the Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025 data set (Edmond). tests/diff_rot/ls_to_edmond_layout.py converts the Larson & Schou 2018 table to it; bin/jsoc_hmi_2010_2026.npz is the mean of the 83 JSOC HMI 72-day inversions (hmi.V_sht_2drls, NACOEFF 36) from 2010-04-30 to 2026-06-29 in this layout, on the 151 table radii. kore projects \(\Omega\) on \(P_0 \dots P_{n_{\max}}\) at each table radius, fits each \(f_n\) in \(r\) over the table radii within 0.01 of the shell, and prints the fit residuals and the truncation error in nHz (the largest difference between the table and its expansion up to \(P_{n_{\max}}\)); check that line. For the Edmond profile the truncation error near the poles at the surface is up to 17 nHz at diff_rot_nmax = 8; 12 is the working choice.

docs.title: Heat equation (thermal = 1)
docs.text:
thermal_wind chooses which entropy terms are added and where the latitudinal background entropy \(S_{tw}\) comes from. The advection of \(s\) by the differential rotation, the first term, is always included.

thermal_wind terms added \(S_{tw}\) 0 \(i\thinspace m G\thinspace \Delta\Omega\thinspace s\) none (e.g. Mirouh et al. 2016) 1 (default) the three terms thermal wind of \(\Omega\) to first order in \(\Delta\Omega\) (\(S_{tw} \propto G^2/\)Beyonce) 2 the three terms thermal wind of the full \((1 + \Delta\Omega)^2\) balance; frame independent 3 the three terms prescribed: \(\partial_\theta S_{tw}\) = dSdtheta \(\sin 2\theta\), uniform in \(r\) (Bekki et al. 2024)
  • thermal_wind 1 and 2 need Beyonce > 0. With timescale = 'rotation', set_scales() sets Beyonce = 0, so set it after calling set_scales().
  • dSdtheta is in the units of \(s\) (\(\delta s/c_p\)): dSdtheta \(= \Delta_\theta s/c_p\), with \(\Delta_\theta s\) in erg g⁻¹ K⁻¹. Bekki et al. use \(c_p\) = 4.17e8, Model S has about 3.46e8. Negative values give warm poles. The thermal-wind amplitude does not apply.
  • thermal_wind_radial = 0 drops \(u_r\thinspace \partial_r S_{tw}\), as Bekki et al. 2022 and Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025 do. Keeping it is the consistent choice, but it moves the solar columnar and high-frequency retrograde modes by 5–15 nHz.
  • With the thermal wind \(S_{tw}\) is the only latitudinal entropy gradient; in a convection zone with \(dS_0/dr = 0\) it is also the only background entropy gradient, and its effect on the modes is of the same order as the momentum terms.
  • ThermaD = 0 works with every option. With thermal_wind ≥ 1 the heat rows are written as \(r^2\thinspace (\mathrm{eq})/p_0\) in a \(C^{(1)}\) basis; see thermad0.md for the caveats (unresolved boundary layer as ThermaD \(\to 0\), small-scale growing modes without diffusion).

docs.title: Resolution and cost
docs.text:
• A differential rotation couples harmonic degrees \(l\) that uniform rotation keeps apart, so the matrices get wider. Let \(n_{\max}\) be the highest degree of \(\Delta\Omega\). The momentum rows then couple degrees that differ by up to \(n_{\max}\) (\(P \to P\), \(T \to T\)) or \(n_{\max} + 1\) (\(P \leftrightarrow T\)).
  • \(S_{tw}\) has degrees up to \(n_{\max} + 2\) (thermal_wind 1) or \(2n_{\max} + 2\) (thermal_wind 2), and the heat rows couple degrees that far apart. Matrices are therefore widest with 'tabulated' and a large diff_rot_nmax.
  • With ricb = 0 (a full sphere) the profiles are evaluated at \(\lvert r\rvert\), to keep them smooth at the centre. 'Y20-wall-bounded' and 'shellular' (except even \(\sigma > 0\)) have a kink at \(r = 0\) and submatrices.py prints a WARNING. The 'solar' tachocline step needs N ≈ 400 at ricb = 0.
  • Check convergence with spin_doctor as for any run; its residuals include the diff-rot terms.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
spin_doctor adds the diff-rot powers to flow.dat (Wdr, Wdr_im, Ensdr) and thermal.dat (Wdr_thm), and writes the options to params.dat, after the general columns (the order is that of spin_doctor.param_table):

diff_rot, diff_rot_ampl, thermal_wind, diff_rot_type, dSdtheta,
diff_rot_term_amp_0, _2, ..., _16, thermal_wind_amplitude, thermal_wind_radial,
diff_rot_frame, diff_rot_nmax, diff_rot_rdeg, diff_rot_generic, diff_rot_solar_0 ... _5,
structure, solar_density_deg, solar_density_window_lo, solar_density_window_hi,
solar_rz, solar_rz_dSdr, solar_rz_x1, solar_rz_x2, solar_rz_d, solar_rz_core, solar_rz_xos, solar_rz_dos,
diff_rot_window, diff_rot_hold, solar_rz_delta_cz, solar_rz_delta_sf, drop_tol, diff_rot_param,
stratification, diffusivity

diff_rot_type is written as its index in diff_rot.TYPES ('Y20' 0, …, 'rigid' 7, 'solar_P4' 8, 'tabulated' 9, 'user' 10); the background columns are described in background.md. A row ends, after a # that np.loadtxt skips, with the 'user' profile definitions and, for 'tabulated', diff_rot_file with the first 12 hex digits of its sha256 (a row with neither has no #). diff_rot_window is 0 for the shell fit and 1 for the whole-Sun fit (with diff_rot_rdeg then the degree used, diff_rot_sun_deg). The column diff_rot_ampl is the former diff_rot_amplitude, and the removed options diff_rot_generic and diff_rot_hold are always 0 and nan, so that the other columns keep their positions; diff_rot_param, stratification and diffusivity are appended at the end. A params.dat written by an older version may have fewer columns; start a new file rather than appending to it. The former names diff_rot_amplitude and diff_rot_generic, and diff_rot_hold (removed on 2026-10-26, differential_rotation_details.md §5.1), stop a run (diff_rot.check).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Conical rotation, Guenel et al. 2016. ricb = 0.71, diff_rot_type = 'conical', diff_rot_ampl = -0.25, \(E = 10^{-5}\), uniform density (structure 'uniform'), stress-free, thermal = 0, \(m = 0\): their DT mode near \(\omega \approx 1.82\); kore gives \(\omega = 1.8173\), \(\sigma = -0.021\).

Solar inertial modes, Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025. The like-for-like set-up of heat-equation.md §8. tests/diff_rot/mk_bekki.py builds it (with keys for \(m\), the profile, the thermal-wind options and \(\Delta_\theta s\)), solve_bekki.py solves it near a target frequency in nHz, and run_bekki.py reproduces the five modes of §8. The parameters it sets:

import units
par.timescale = 'rotation'; par.set_scales()
par.structure = 'old model S prototype'                  # the Model S density (background.md)
par.r_out = 0.985; par.ricb = 0.71/0.985                 # shell 0.71-0.985 R☉
par.stratification = 'odd top hat'                       # with A = aux5 = 0: dS0/dr = 0 (δ = 0)
par.aux1, par.aux2, par.aux3, par.aux4, par.aux5 = 0.0, 0.1, 0.68, 0.06, 0.0
par.thermal = 1; par.bci = par.bco = 0; par.bci_thermal = par.bco_thermal = 1
par.diff_rot = 1; par.diff_rot_type = 'tabulated'; par.diff_rot_file = 'diff_rot.npz'
par.diff_rot_nmax = 12
par.thermal_wind = 2; par.thermal_wind_radial = 0
units.set_physical(par, frame_nHz=456.0, nu=1e12, kappa=1e12)   # Gaspard, Beyonce, ViscosD, ThermaD, diff_rot_frame
par.N = 64; par.lmax = par.m + 63

The \(m = 1\) high-latitude mode comes out at −95.76 nHz with growth rate +11.30 nHz (theirs: −95.70, +11.69); the table in heat-equation.md §8 has more modes. With thermal_wind = 3 and dSdtheta \(= \Delta_\theta s/c_p\) the same set-up gives the baroclinic onset of Bekki et al. 2024 (\(\lvert\Delta_\theta s\rvert \approx 425\) erg g⁻¹ K⁻¹ with the Edmond \(\Omega\)).

docs.title: Differential rotation in kore: physics, equations and implementation
docs.text:
This page is a self-contained reference for the differential rotation of kore's anelastic_log branch. It covers:

  • the physics: what a differentially rotating background does to a linear perturbation (§1);
  • the anelastic (LBR) equations with differential rotation, and the derivation of every term that the differential rotation adds to the momentum and heat equations (§2);
  • the spectral form of these terms: how they couple spherical-harmonic degrees, and how the angular coupling coefficients are obtained (§3);
  • the implementation, term by term: radial profiles, operator labels, the operators, the assembly of the matrices and the diagnostics (§4 to §8);
  • the internal consistency checks built into the code, and the known limitations (§9, §10);
  • benchmarks against published eigenvalues: Baruteau & Rieutord 2013, Guenel et al. 2016, Mirouh et al. 2016, Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025a and 2025b (§11);
  • the cost in time and memory against the highest degree of \(\Delta\Omega\) (§12).

It describes the code after the differential rotation was unified in bin/diff_rot.py on the angular algebra of bin/angular.py (2026-10-23, on top of commit b4598010). The code references give a file and a function, and a line number in that version (line numbers drift; the function names do not).

Contents

  • 0. Notation and code names
  • 1. Physics
  • 2. Equations
  • 3. Spectral form
  • 4. Implementation overview
  • 5. Radial profiles
  • 6. Radial operators and labels
  • 7. The operators and the assembly
  • 8. Diagnostics
  • 9. Internal consistency checks
  • 10. Limitations
  • 11. Benchmarks against published results
  • 12. Cost against the highest degree

docs.title: 0. Notation and code names
docs.text:
Everything is dimensionless. The length unit is the outer radius \(r_0\) (r = 1 at the outer boundary), and the time unit is \(\tau\), chosen by par.timescale ('rotation' gives \(\tau = 1/\Omega_{\rm ref}\)).

symbol meaning in the code \(r, \theta, \phi\); \(x\) spherical coordinates; \(x = \cos\theta\) \(\varpi\) cylindrical radius \(r\sin\theta\) \(\hat{\mathbf z}\) rotation axis \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\) rotation rate of the frame in which kore solves diff_rot_frame (nHz) for the solar profiles \(G\) \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\tau\), the frame's rotation rate in time units par.Gaspard \(\Delta\Omega(r,\theta)\) relative differential rotation, \(\Omega = \Omega_{\rm ref}(1 + \Delta\Omega)\) par.diff_rot_type \(f_n(r)\) Legendre coefficients of \(\Delta\Omega\): \(\Delta\Omega = \sum_n f_n(r) P_n(x)\), \(n\) even (diff_rot_ampl times \(a_n\) (diff_rot_term_amp) times the shape of the type) zf0, zf2, zf4, …; zd, zs for \(rf_n'\), \(r^2f_n''\) \(\mathbf U_0\) the background flow seen in the rotating frame \(\rho_0, T_0\) background density and temperature prf.density \(h\) \(\ln\rho_0\) profile code lho \(p_0\) \(\rho_0 T_0\) (not the pressure) pss \(g(r)\) gravity gra \(S_0(r)\) spherical background entropy, in units of \(c_p\); \(S_0'\) its gradient dSd (\(S_0'\)), pdS (\(p_0 S_0'\)) \(S_{tw}(r,\theta)\) latitudinal background entropy (thermal wind, or prescribed) \(\sigma_n(r)\) Legendre coefficients of \(S_{tw}\) tw2 = \(p_0\sigma_2\), tp2 = \(p_0\sigma_2'\), … \(\nu, \kappa\) viscosity and thermal diffusivity profiles vsc, kps = \(\kappa p_0\) Beyonce \((N_0\tau)^2\): the buoyancy force is \(\mathrm{Beyonce}\thinspace g s \hat{\mathbf r}\) par.Beyonce ViscosD, ThermaD \(\nu_0\tau/r_0^2\), \(\kappa_0\tau/r_0^2\) par.ViscosD, par.ThermaD \(\mathbf u\), \(s\) velocity and entropy perturbation (\(s = \delta s/c_p\)) \(P, T\) poloidal and toroidal scalars of \(\mathbf u\) sections u and v \(m\) azimuthal order: fields go as \(e^{i m\phi}\) par.m \(l\), \(L\) harmonic degree, \(L = l(l+1)\) l \(l'\), \(l\) target degree (row) and source degree (column) of a coupling l, l + offdiag in operators.py \(Y_l\) Schmidt-normalised spherical harmonic \(Y_l^m\), \(\int\lvert Y_l\rvert^2 d\Omega = n_l = 4\pi/(2l+1)\) utils.Ylm \(\lambda\) eigenvalue, fields \(\propto e^{\lambda t}\), \(\lambda = \sigma + i\omega\) (\(\omega < 0\) is prograde)

Two code conventions recur everywhere:

  • Sections. The unknowns and the matrix rows are stacked in blocks: section u holds the rows of the radial component of the double curl of the momentum equation (one row block per poloidal degree), section v the rows of the radial component of its curl (one per toroidal degree), and section h the heat equation (one per degree of \(s\), which follows the poloidal degrees).
  • Row weights. Each row is multiplied by a power of \(r\) and of \(\rho_0\), chosen so that every radial coefficient is a polynomial, and divided by \(L'^3\), where \(l'\) is the row degree.

docs.title: 1.1 The background
docs.text:
kore solves in a frame rotating at the constant rate \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\). The background rotates at

\[ \Omega(r,\theta) = \Omega_{\rm ref}\left[1 + \Delta\Omega(r,\theta)\right], \qquad \Delta\Omega = \sum_{n = 0, 2, 4, \dots} f_n(r) P_n(\cos\theta) . \]

Only even \(n\) appear, so the rotation is symmetric about the equator, and the equatorial symmetry of the modes (par.symm) still separates the problem into two classes. In the rotating frame the differential rotation is a steady azimuthal flow

\[ \mathbf U_0 = G\thinspace \Delta\Omega\thinspace r\sin\theta\thinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi = G\thinspace \Delta\Omega\thinspace \hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf r . \qquad (1.1) \]

The factor \(G\) = Gaspard converts the rotation rate \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\Delta\Omega\) to the time unit \(\tau\). It is 1 when \(\tau = 1/\Omega_{\rm ref}\). \(G\) does not choose the frame: \(\Delta\Omega\) is defined relative to the frame, and for the solar profiles the frame rate is set by diff_rot_frame (or fixed at 435 nHz for 'solar').

The spherical background (\(\rho_0\), \(T_0\), \(g\), \(S_0\), \(\nu\), \(\kappa\)) is the same as without differential rotation. The differential rotation adds only two things: the flow \(\mathbf U_0\), and a latitudinal entropy \(S_{tw}(r,\theta)\) (§1.3).

docs.title: 1.2 What the differential rotation does to a perturbation
docs.text:
A perturbation \(\mathbf u\) is carried by the background flow and sheared by it. Linearising the advection \((\mathbf U_0 + \mathbf u)\cdot\nabla(\mathbf U_0 + \mathbf u)\) gives (§2.3) three effects:

  1. Advection at the local rotation rate. A pattern \(e^{i m\phi}\) is carried round at the local rate \(G\Delta\Omega\), which shifts its frequency by \(-m G\Delta\Omega\) locally. With uniform \(\Delta\Omega\) this is just a Doppler shift.
  2. Coriolis force of the local rotation. The Coriolis parameter becomes \(2G(1 + \Delta\Omega)\) instead of \(2G\). Together with (1), a uniform \(\Delta\Omega\) is exactly a change of frame (§2.6).
  3. Transport across the shear. A perturbation that moves across the gradient of \(\Omega\) carries its angular momentum to a place where the background rotates at a different rate. This is the term \(r\sin\theta\thinspace (\mathbf u\cdot\nabla\Delta\Omega)\thinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi\). It is the only term through which the perturbation can exchange kinetic energy with the background flow (§2.3), so it is what drives shear instabilities.

In the heat equation the entropy perturbation is advected by \(\mathbf U_0\) (the same Doppler shift for \(s\)), and the perturbation velocity advects the latitudinal background entropy \(S_{tw}\).

docs.title: 1.3 Thermal-wind balance
docs.text:
A rotation rate that varies along the rotation axis cannot be balanced by pressure alone. The centrifugal force of the differential rotation then has a curl, and in a stratified fluid only a buoyancy force that varies with latitude, that is a latitudinal entropy gradient, can balance it. This is thermal-wind balance. A differentially rotating star in equilibrium therefore has a background entropy \(S_0(r) + S_{tw}(r,\theta)\). kore computes \(S_{tw}\) from \(\Delta\Omega\) (thermal_wind 1 or 2), prescribes it (thermal_wind = 3), or omits it (thermal_wind = 0).

\(S_{tw}\) is small in amplitude, since it scales as \(G^2/(\mathrm{Beyonce}\thinspace g)\). But the buoyancy it produces through a perturbation scales as \(\mathrm{Beyonce}\thinspace g\thinspace s\). The product does not depend on Beyonce: the feedback of \(S_{tw}\) on the motion is of order \(\Delta\Omega\) relative to the Coriolis force, the same order as the momentum terms of §1.2. In a convection zone, where \(S_0' \approx 0\), \(S_{tw}\) is the only background entropy gradient, and the meridional flow of a perturbation across it (the baroclinic coupling) can destabilise modes.

docs.title: 1.4 What is not modelled
docs.text:
• The background is imposed and fixed: nothing maintains \(\Omega\) or \(S_{tw}\) against viscosity or diffusion, and the perturbation equations have no source terms for them.
  • \(\rho_0\), \(T_0\) and \(g\) stay spherical: no centrifugal distortion, no latitudinal variation of \(\rho_0 T_0\) or \(g\) induced by the thermal wind, and no thermal-wind density in the mass flux. These effects are of relative size \(\Delta\Omega/(\mathrm{Beyonce}\thinspace g)\).
  • The thermal wind is the one consistent with LBR buoyancy. The full anelastic balance would add a term \(p_b S_0'/(\rho_0 g)\) to \(S_{tw}\) (\(p_b\) the background pressure perturbation), the analogue of the \(p_1 S_0'\) term that LBR drops for the perturbations. It matters only where \(S_0' \neq 0\).
  • There is no magnetic field and no viscous heating.

docs.title: 2.1 The linear anelastic (LBR) equations
docs.text:
In the frame rotating at \(\Omega_{ m ref}\), with the background of §1.1, a perturbation \((\mathbf u, s)\) obeys, per unit mass (Lantz–Braginsky–Roberts form, with \(\varpi'\) the reduced pressure \(p'/ ho_0\)):

\[ rac{\partial\mathbf u}{\partial t} + 2G hinspace \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u + \mathbf W(\mathbf u) = - abla\varpi' + \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace s hinspace \hat{\mathbf r} + \mathrm{ViscosD} hinspace \mathbf F_ u(\mathbf u), \qquad (2.1) \] \[ abla\cdot( ho_0\mathbf u) = 0, \qquad (2.2) \] \[ p_0\left[ rac{\partial s}{\partial t} + \mathbf U_0\cdot abla s + u_r S_0' + \mathbf u\cdot abla S_{tw} ight] = \mathrm{ThermaD} hinspace abla\cdot(\kappa hinspace p_0 abla s). \qquad (2.3) \]

Here \(\mathbf F_ u = ho_0^{-1} abla\cdot( ho_0 u hinspace \mathsf S)\) is the viscous force of the anelastic stress tensor \(\mathsf S\), and

\[ \mathbf W(\mathbf u) = (\mathbf U_0\cdot abla)\mathbf u + (\mathbf u\cdot abla)\mathbf U_0 \qquad (2.4) \]

is the linearised advection by the background flow. Without differential rotation, \(\mathbf W = 0\), \(\mathbf U_0\cdot abla s = 0\) and \(S_{tw} = 0\), and (2.1)–(2.3) are kore's standard equations. The differential rotation adds exactly three terms: \(\mathbf W\) in (2.1), and \(p_0\mathbf U_0\cdot abla s\) and \(p_0\mathbf u\cdot abla S_{tw}\) in (2.3).

Remarks:

  • In LBR form the buoyancy depends on \(s\) only. The reduced pressure is a gradient, so it disappears when the curl of (2.1) is taken (§3.2): kore never solves for it.
  • The viscous force, the buoyancy and the diffusion are not changed by the differential rotation.
  • (2.2) is satisfied exactly by the poloidal–toroidal form of \(\mathbf u\) (§3.1).

kore solves the eigenvalue problem for fields \(\propto e^{\lambda t + i m\phi}\), so \(\partial_t o \lambda\) and \(\partial_\phi o i m\).

docs.title: 2.2 The background flow as a local rotation
docs.text:
Write the background rotation in time units as \(\Omega_d(r,\theta) = G\Delta\Omega\), so that \(\mathbf U_0 = \Omega_d\thinspace \hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf r\). Two identities are used below:

\[ \mathbf U_0\cdot\nabla = \Omega_d\thinspace \partial_\phi, \qquad (\mathbf v\cdot\nabla)(\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf r) = \hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf v , \]

for any vector \(\mathbf v\). In components, with \(\hat{\mathbf z} = \cos\theta\thinspace \hat{\mathbf r} - \sin\theta\thinspace \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\),

\[ \hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf u = \left(-\sin\theta\thinspace u_\phi,\ -\cos\theta\thinspace u_\phi,\ \sin\theta\thinspace u_r + \cos\theta\thinspace u_\theta\right) \qquad (2.5) \]

in the \((\hat{\mathbf r}, \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}, \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi)\) basis.

docs.title: 2.3 Derivation of the momentum term
docs.text:
Advection of the perturbation by \(\mathbf U_0\). \((\mathbf U_0\cdot abla)\mathbf u = \Omega_d hinspace \partial_\phi\mathbf u\), where \(\partial_\phi\) also acts on the unit vectors: \(\partial_\phi\hat{\mathbf r} = \sin heta hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi\), \(\partial_\phi\hat{ oldsymbol heta} = \cos heta hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi\), \(\partial_\phi\hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi = -\sin heta hinspace \hat{\mathbf r} - \cos heta hinspace \hat{ oldsymbol heta}\). With (2.5) this is

\[ (\mathbf U_0\cdot abla)\mathbf u = \Omega_d\left[i m hinspace \mathbf u + \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u ight], \]

where \(i m hinspace \mathbf u\) means \(i m\) times each component.

Advection of \(\mathbf U_0\) by the perturbation.

\[ (\mathbf u\cdot abla)\mathbf U_0 = (\mathbf u\cdot abla\Omega_d) hinspace \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf r + \Omega_d hinspace (\mathbf u\cdot abla)(\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf r) = r\sin heta hinspace (\mathbf u\cdot abla\Omega_d) hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi + \Omega_d hinspace \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u . \]

Sum. With \(\mathbf u\cdot abla\Delta\Omega = u_r\partial_r\Delta\Omega + (u_ heta/r)\partial_ heta\Delta\Omega\),

\[ \mathbf W = G\left[\Delta\Omega\left(i m hinspace \mathbf u + 2\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u ight) + \sin heta\left(r hinspace \partial_r\Delta\Omega hinspace u_r + \partial_ heta\Delta\Omega hinspace u_ heta ight)\hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi ight]. \qquad (2.6) \]

This is the force that operators.differential_rotation discretises. The three parts are those of §1.2: the Doppler term \(i m\Delta\Omega hinspace \mathbf u\); the Coriolis force of the local rotation \(2\Delta\Omega hinspace \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u\), which adds to the frame's \(2\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u\); and the shear term.

For \(\Delta\Omega = f(r)P_n(x)\), using \(\partial_ heta P_n(\cos heta) = -\sin heta hinspace P_n'(x)\), the components are

\[ egin{aligned} W_r/G &= f P_n\left[i m hinspace u_r - 2\sin heta hinspace u_\phi ight],\cr W_ heta/G &= f P_n\left[i m hinspace u_ heta - 2x hinspace u_\phi ight],\cr W_\phi/G &= f P_n\left[i m hinspace u_\phi + 2\sin heta hinspace u_r + 2x hinspace u_ heta ight] + \sin heta\left[(r f') hinspace P_n hinspace u_r - f\sin heta hinspace P_n' hinspace u_ heta ight]. \end{aligned} \qquad (2.7) \]

The profile enters only as \(f\) and \(r f'\); the second derivative \(r^2 f''\) appears later, when the double curl differentiates \(W\) in \(r\) (§3.4).

Energy. For a mode, \(2 hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int ho_0 hinspace \mathbf u^\ast\cdot\mathbf W hinspace dV\) is the rate at which \(\mathbf W\) removes kinetic energy. The Doppler part gives \(i m\int ho_0\Delta\Omega\lvert\mathbf u vert^2 dV\), which is imaginary. The Coriolis part gives \(\mathbf u^\ast\cdot(\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u) = \hat{\mathbf z}\cdot(\mathbf u imes\mathbf u^\ast)\), which is also imaginary. Only the shear term, \(2G hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int ho_0 hinspace r\sin heta hinspace u_\phi^\ast hinspace (\mathbf u\cdot abla\Delta\Omega) hinspace dV\), exchanges energy with the background. These parts shift the frequency (residω) or change the growth rate (residσ) in spin_doctor (§8).

docs.title: 2.4 Thermal-wind entropy
docs.text:
The balance. The steady background satisfies, in the rotating frame and per unit mass,

\[ (\mathbf U_0\cdot abla)\mathbf U_0 + 2G hinspace \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf U_0 = - abla\varpi_b + \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace S_{tw} hinspace \hat{\mathbf r}, \]

where \(\varpi_b\) collects the pressure and gravity potential terms. With \(\mathbf U_0 = \Omega_d hinspace \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf r\), the left side is \(-(\Omega_d^2 + 2G\Omega_d) hinspace \varpi hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \varpi = -G^2\left[(1 + \Delta\Omega)^2 - 1 ight]\varpi hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \varpi\), the centrifugal and Coriolis forces of the differential rotation (\(\hat{\mathbf e}_ \varpi\) the cylindrical radial unit vector). The \(\phi\)-component of the curl removes \(\varpi_b\). Using \(( abla imes F\hat{\mathbf e}_ \varpi)_ \phi = \partial_z F\) and \(( abla imes F\hat{\mathbf r})_ \phi = -r^{-1}\partial_ heta F\),

\[ rac{1}{r} rac{\partial S_{tw}}{\partial heta} = rac{G^2 hinspace r\sin heta}{\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g} hinspace rac{\partial (1 + \Delta\Omega)^2}{\partial z}, \qquad rac{\partial}{\partial z} = \cos heta hinspace rac{\partial}{\partial r} - rac{\sin heta}{r} rac{\partial}{\partial heta}. \qquad (2.8) \]

In the variable \(x\). With \(\partial_ heta = -\sin heta hinspace \partial_x\) and \(\partial_z = x\partial_r + r^{-1}(1 - x^2)\partial_x\), (2.8) becomes

\[ rac{\partial S_{tw}}{\partial x} = - rac{r^2 G^2}{\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g}\left[x hinspace rac{\partial F}{\partial r} + rac{1 - x^2}{r} rac{\partial F}{\partial x} ight], \qquad F = egin{cases} 2\Delta\Omega & ext{(linear)} \cr (1 + \Delta\Omega)^2 - 1 & ext{(exact)} \end{cases} \qquad (2.9) \]

thermal_wind = 1 uses the linear form, thermal_wind = 2 the exact one. Only the exact form is independent of the frame: \(G^2(1 + \Delta\Omega)^2\) is the square of the physical rotation rate, the same whatever \(\Omega_{ m ref}\) the profile is written against, whereas \(G^2\cdot 2\Delta\Omega\) is \(2\Omega_{ m ref}(\Omega - \Omega_{ m ref}) au^2\) and changes with the frame. With thermal_wind = 1 the modes therefore move with the choice of frame, at second order in \(\Delta\Omega\).

The right side of (2.9) is a polynomial in \(x\) of degree \(n_{\max} + 1\) (linear) or \(2n_{\max} + 1\) (exact), so \(S_{tw} = \sum_n \sigma_n(r) P_n(x)\) has even degrees up to \(n_{\max} + 2\) or \(2n_{\max} + 2\). The \(l = 0\) part \(\sigma_0\) is a spherical entropy, absorbed in \(S_0\), and set to zero.

Closed forms for \(\Delta\Omega = f_0 + f_2 P_2\). Writing the bracket of (2.9) on \(P_1\) and \(P_3\) (with \(x P_2 = frac{3}{5}P_3 + frac{2}{5}P_1\), \(3x(1 - x^2) = frac{6}{5}(P_1 - P_3)\), \(P_2' = 3P_1\), \(P_4' = 7P_3 + 3P_1\)) and matching coefficients gives, with \(e = 0\) for thermal_wind = 1 and \(e = 1\) for thermal_wind = 2,

\[ egin{aligned} \sigma_2 &= - rac{2r^2G^2}{\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g}\left[(1 + e f_0)\left( rac{f_0'}{3} + rac{f_2'}{21} + rac{4}{7} rac{f_2}{r} ight) + rac{e hinspace f_2 (f_0' + f_2')}{21} ight],\cr \sigma_4 &= - rac{6r^2G^2}{35 hinspace \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g}\left[(1 + e f_0)\left(f_2' - rac{2f_2}{r} ight) + e\left(f_2 f_0' + rac{4}{11}f_2 f_2' + rac{14}{11} rac{f_2^2}{r} ight) ight],\cr \sigma_6 &= -e hinspace rac{4r^2G^2}{77 hinspace \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g} hinspace f_2\left(f_2' - rac{2f_2}{r} ight). \end{aligned} \qquad (2.10) \]

kore computes the \(\sigma_n\) from (2.9) by the Legendre-series algebra of §5.4, for any degrees of \(\Delta\Omega\); (2.10) is kept as a validation (tests/diff_rot/gen_check.py, §9). Two analytic checks:

  • Cylindrical rotation, \(\Delta\Omega = \varepsilon\varpi^2\), i.e. \(f_0 = frac{2}{3}\varepsilon r^2\), \(f_2 = - frac{2}{3}\varepsilon r^2\): \(\sigma_2 = \sigma_4 = \sigma_6 = 0\). A rotation constant on cylinders is barotropic and needs no thermal wind.
  • Conical rotation, \(\Delta\Omega = \varepsilon\sin^2 heta\), i.e. \(f_0 = frac{2}{3}\varepsilon\), \(f_2 = - frac{2}{3}\varepsilon\) (linear form): \(\sigma_2 = 16\varepsilon r/(21 hinspace\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g)\), \(\sigma_4 = -8\varepsilon r/(35 hinspace\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g)\), and \(S_{tw}( ext{pole}) - S_{tw}( ext{equator}) = \varepsilon r/(\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g)\): an equator rotating faster (\(\varepsilon > 0\)) needs warmer poles.

Prescribed latitudinal entropy (thermal_wind = 3). \(\partial_ heta S_{tw}\) = dSdtheta \(\sin 2 heta\), independent of \(\Omega\) and of \(r\). Since \(\sin 2 heta = - frac{2}{3} hinspace dP_2/d heta\),

\[ \sigma_2 = - frac{2}{3} hinspace exttt{dSdtheta}, \qquad \sigma_n = 0 \quad (n \ge 4). \]

dSdtheta is in the units of \(s\) (\(\delta s/c_p\)); negative values give warm poles. \(\Omega\) still enters through \(\mathbf W\) and the advection of \(s\). For a uniformly rotating background with a prescribed \(S_{tw}\), use diff_rot_type = 'rigid' with diff_rot_ampl = 0.

docs.title: 2.5 The heat-equation terms
docs.text:
\(S_{tw}\) does not depend on \(\phi\), so \(\mathbf U_0\cdot\nabla S_{tw} = 0\), and \(\mathbf U_0\cdot\nabla s = G\Delta\Omega\thinspace \partial_\phi s\). The left side of (2.3) gains

\[ p_0\left[\thinspace \underbrace{i m G\Delta\Omega\thinspace s}_ {\text{(a) advection}} + \underbrace{u_r\frac{\partial S_{tw}}{\partial r}}_ {\text{(b) radial}} + \underbrace{\frac{u_\theta}{r}\frac{\partial S_{tw}}{\partial\theta}}_ {\text{(c) latitudinal}}\thinspace \right]. \qquad (2.11) \]

(a) is always included. (b) and (c) are included for thermal_wind 1, 2, 3; thermal_wind_radial = 0 drops (b). (a) is anti-Hermitian under the entropy pairing \(\int s^\ast(\cdot)\thinspace dV\), so it only shifts the frequency; (b) and (c) exchange entropy variance with the flow.

docs.title: 2.6 An exact result: the rigid offset
docs.text:
For a uniform \(\Delta\Omega = a\) (diff_rot_type = 'rigid'), \(\partial\Delta\Omega = 0\), \(S_{tw} = 0\), and (2.6) and (2.11) reduce to \(G a(i m\mathbf u + 2\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf u)\) and \(i m G a\thinspace p_0 s\). Equations (2.1) and (2.3) become those of uniform rotation at rate \(G(1 + a)\), with \(\lambda\) replaced by \(\lambda + i m G a\). So

\[ \lambda(a, G) = \lambda_0\big(G(1 + a)\big) - i m G a , \qquad (2.12) \]

where \(\lambda_0(G)\) is the eigenvalue without differential rotation. This identity tests the Doppler and Coriolis parts of the operators and their signs (§9).

docs.title: 3.1 Fields
docs.text:
At fixed \(m\) and equatorial symmetry, each field is a sum over degrees,

\[ \mathbf u = \sum_l\left[ ho_0^{-1} abla imes abla imes( ho_0 P_l Y_l hinspace \mathbf r) + abla imes(T_l Y_l hinspace \mathbf r) ight], \qquad s = \sum_l s_l Y_l , \]

where \(P\) and \(s\) use the poloidal degrees and \(T\) the toroidal ones (utils.ell(m, lmax, symm) returns both lists). This form satisfies (2.2) exactly. For one degree, with \(Z_l = i m Y_l/\sin heta\) and

\[ a_l = rac{(r P_l)'}{r} + h' P_l = rac{P_l}{r} + P_l' + h' P_l , \qquad (3.1) \]

the components are

\[ u_r = rac{L P_l}{r} Y_l, \qquad u_ heta = a_l hinspace \partial_ heta Y_l + T_l Z_l, \qquad u_\phi = a_l Z_l - T_l hinspace \partial_ heta Y_l . \qquad (3.2) \]

These expressions underlie diff_rot._primitives (through the basis fields of §3.3), utils4pp.diff_rot_setup and ru_insane.py.

docs.title: 3.2 Projection of a vector field, and kore's rows
docs.text:
Any vector field \(\mathbf F\) is projected on vector spherical harmonics as

\[ \mathbf F = \sum_l\left[F^q_l hinspace Y_l hinspace \hat{\mathbf r} + F^s_l hinspace r abla Y_l + F^t_l hinspace r abla Y_l imes\hat{\mathbf r} ight], \qquad r abla Y = \partial_ heta Y hinspace \hat{ oldsymbol heta} + Z hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi, \quad r abla Y imes\hat{\mathbf r} = Z hinspace \hat{ oldsymbol heta} - \partial_ heta Y hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi , \qquad (3.3) \]

with, since \(\int(\lvert\partial_ heta Y_l vert^2 + \lvert Z_l vert^2) hinspace d\Omega = L n_l\),

\[ F^q_l = rac{1}{n_l}\int F_r Y_l^\ast hinspace d\Omega, \qquad F^s_l = rac{1}{L n_l}\int\left(F_ heta hinspace \partial_ heta Y_l^\ast + F_\phi Z_l^\ast ight)d\Omega, \qquad F^t_l = rac{1}{L n_l}\int\left(F_ heta Z_l^\ast - F_\phi hinspace \partial_ heta Y_l^\ast ight)d\Omega . \qquad (3.4) \]

By (3.2) the velocity has \(u^q = L P/r\), \(u^s = a\), \(u^t = T\).

Taking curls removes the pressure:

\[ \hat{\mathbf r}\cdot abla imes\mathbf F = \sum_l rac{L}{r}F^t_l Y_l, \qquad \hat{\mathbf r}\cdot abla imes abla imes\mathbf F = \sum_l rac{L}{r^2}\left[F^q_l - \partial_r(r F^s_l) ight]Y_l . \qquad (3.5) \]

(The toroidal part \(F^t r abla Y imes\hat{\mathbf r} = abla imes(F^t Y\mathbf r)\) has no radial curl-curl, and the spheroidal part \(F^q Y\hat{\mathbf r} + F^s r abla Y\) has the curl \(r^{-1}\left[F^q - \partial_r(r F^s) ight] r abla Y imes\hat{\mathbf r}\).)

kore's rows of degree \(l'\) are (3.5) multiplied by \(r^{ m rpower} ho_0^{ m rhopower}\) and divided by \(L'^3\). With the defaults rpower_u = 5, rpower_v = 3, rhopower_u = rhopower_v = 1:

\[ \mathrm{row}_ u(\mathbf F) = rac{r^3 ho_0}{L'^2}\left[F^q_{l'} - \partial_r(r F^s_{l'}) ight], \qquad \mathrm{row}_ v(\mathbf F) = rac{r^2 ho_0}{L'^2}F^t_{l'} . \qquad (3.6) \]

For example, \(\mathbf F = \mathbf u\) gives \(\mathrm{row}_ u = \left[L r^2 ho_0 P - r^3 ho_0(2P' + rP'' + h'P + r h'' P + r h' P') ight]/L^2\) and \(\mathrm{row}_ v = r^2 ho_0 T/L^2\), which is operators.inertia (line 26). The diff-rot operator is (3.6) applied to \(\mathbf W\).

docs.title: 3.3 Angular primitives
docs.text:
Insert one source degree \(l\) of (3.2) into (2.7), with \(\Delta\Omega = f(r)P_n(x)\). Each component of \(\mathbf W\) is a sum of four radial "shapes" times angular functions:

shape radial factor from q \(f hinspace L P_l/r\) \(u_r\) with \(f\) a \(f hinspace a_l\) the consoidal part of \(u_ heta\), \(u_\phi\) T \(f hinspace T_l\) the toroidal part dq \((r f') hinspace L P_l/r\) \(u_r\) in the shear term

From (2.7) and (3.2), the angular functions, per unit \(G\) and per unit shape, are (\(Y = Y_l\), \(Z = Z_l\)):

shape \(W_r\) \(W_ heta\) \(W_\phi\) q \(i m P_n Y\) 0 \(2\sin heta hinspace P_n Y\) a \(-2 i m P_n Y\) \(P_n(i m hinspace \partial_ heta Y - 2xZ)\) \(P_n(i m Z + 2x hinspace \partial_ heta Y) - \sin^2 heta hinspace P_n' hinspace \partial_ heta Y\) T \(2\sin heta hinspace P_n hinspace \partial_ heta Y\) \(P_n(i m Z + 2x hinspace \partial_ heta Y)\) \(P_n(-i m hinspace \partial_ heta Y + 2xZ) - \sin^2 heta hinspace P_n' Z\) dq 0 0 \(\sin heta hinspace P_n Y\)

Projecting each entry on the target degree \(l'\) with (3.4) defines twelve matrices \(C^k_{ m sh}[l', l]\), with \(k \in \lbrace q, s, t brace\) the projection and sh the shape. Then, for the target degree \(l'\),

\[ W^k_{l'} = G\sum_l\left[C^k_q hinspace f rac{L_l P_l}{r} + C^k_a hinspace f a_l + C^k_T hinspace f T_l + C^k_{dq} hinspace (r f') rac{L_l P_l}{r} ight]. \qquad (3.7) \]

The angular algebra. The \(C^k_{ m sh}\) are not computed by integration but built exactly, as sparse products of a few matrices on the degree index (bin/angular.py). Multiplying a field by a function of \(x\) maps degree \(l\) to a few neighbouring degrees, by two exact recurrences of the Schmidt harmonics (\(p_l\), \(q_l\) as in (3.8) below):

\[ x hinspace Y_l = p_l Y_{l+1} + q_l Y_{l-1} \quad o X, \qquad (1 - x^2) rac{dY_l}{dx} = -\sin heta hinspace \partial_ heta Y_l = (l+1)q_l Y_{l-1} - l p_l Y_{l+1} \quad o D , \]

with rows the target degree and columns the source degree. Their adjoints under \(\int d\Omega\) (with \(N = \mathrm{diag}(n_l)\)) are \(X^\dagger = N^{-1}X^{ m T}N = X\) and \(D^\dagger = N^{-1}D^{ m T}N = 2X - D\) (integration by parts). \(P_n(X)\) and \(P_n'(X)\) follow from the three-term recurrences \((k+1)P_{k+1} = (2k+1)XP_k - kP_{k-1}\), \(P_{k+1}' = (k+1)P_k + XP_k'\). Write \(R_l = Y_l\hat{\mathbf r}\), \(S_l = r abla Y_l\), \(T_l = r abla Y_l imes\hat{\mathbf r}\) for the basis fields of (3.3), \(L\) for \(\mathrm{diag}(l(l+1))\) acting on the source and \(1/L'\) for the division of each row by its \(L'\) (0 for \(l' = 0\)). The operations needed by (2.7) are then:

operation result on \((q, s, t)\) from \(g(x) hinspace R_l\) \(q\): \(g(X)\) \(g(x) hinspace S_l\) \(s\): \((g(X)L - g'(X)D)/L'\), \(t\): \(-i m hinspace g'(X)/L'\) \(\int g abla Y_l\cdot abla Y_{l'}^\ast = \int Y_{l'}^\ast(L_l g Y_l - g' DY_l)\) \(g(x) hinspace T_l\) \(s\): \(i m hinspace g'(X)/L'\), \(t\): \((g(X)L - g'(X)D)/L'\) the same, rotated by \(\hat{\mathbf r} imes\) \(\hat{\mathbf z} imes(c hinspace Y\hat{\mathbf r})\) \(s\): \(-i m hinspace c/L'\), \(t\): \(D^\dagger c/L'\) \(\hat{\mathbf z} imes\hat{\mathbf r} = \sin heta hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi\) \(\hat{\mathbf z} imes S_l\) \(-i m R_l - x T_l\) (2.5) \(\hat{\mathbf z} imes T_l\) \(-(DY_l)\hat{\mathbf r} + x S_l\) (2.5) \(\sin heta hinspace F_ heta\) (a scalar) \(-D s + i m hinspace t\) \(\sin heta hinspace \partial_ heta Y = -DY\)

diff_rot._primitives (line 324) composes them, per unit \(G\) and per unit shape:

\[ \mathbf W_{ m sh} = P_n(x)\left[i m hinspace \mathbf u_{ m sh} + 2\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u_{ m sh} ight] + \hat{\mathbf z} imes\left[-P_n'(x)\sin heta hinspace u_{ heta,{ m sh}} hinspace \hat{\mathbf r} ight], \qquad \mathbf W_{dq} = \hat{\mathbf z} imes\left[P_n(x) hinspace Y\hat{\mathbf r} ight], \]

with \(\mathbf u_q = R_l\), \(\mathbf u_a = S_l\), \(\mathbf u_T = T_l\) (the second term, the \(u_ heta\) part of the shear term, vanishes for the shape q). Every product is a sparse product of banded matrices, so the cost is \(O(l_{\max})\) and the result is exact to round-off at any degree. The matrices are built up to \(l_w\) = lmax + n + 6, because a product of matrices truncated at \(l_w\) is wrong only in its last few degrees.

The primitives were first computed by Gauss–Legendre quadrature of the table above; that builder is kept as an independent reference in tests/diff_rot/quad_reference.py. It cost \(O(l_{\max}^3)\) (177 s at lmax 1025) and failed silently from \(l = 646\) on, where scipy.special.sph_harm_y returns NaN; the two agree to \(\sim 10^{-12}\) below that (§9).

docs.title: 3.4 From the primitives to the radial operators
docs.text:
Put (3.7) into (3.6) and expand \(a_l\) with (3.1). For the \(v\) rows this is direct:

\[ \mathrm{row}_ v(\mathbf W) = \frac{G r^2\rho_0}{L'^2}\left[(L_l C^t_q + C^t_a)\frac{fP}{r} + C^t_a\thinspace f(P' + h'P) + C^t_T\thinspace f T + L_l C^t_{dq}\frac{(rf')P}{r}\right]. \]

For the \(u\) rows, \(\partial_r(r W^s)\) differentiates the profile and the unknowns: with \(r a = P + rP' + r h' P\),

\[ \partial_r(r f a) = f'(P + rP' + rh'P) + f(2P' + rP'' + h'P + rh''P + rh'P'), \qquad \partial_r\left(r\thinspace C_{dq}^s (rf')\frac{L_lP}{r}\right) = L_l C^s_{dq}\left[(f' + r f'')P + (rf')P'\right], \]

which is where \(r^2 f''\) enters. Collecting the coefficient of each radial operator gives the table below. Each coefficient is a matrix in \((l', l)\), and in the code it is stored multiplied by \(L'\); the operator then divides by \(L'^3\) (§7.1), so the net factor is \(1/L'^2\) as in (3.6). The radial operators include the row weights, and their labels (§6) use the profile codes {a}, {s}, {p} of \(f_n\), \(r f_n'\), \(r^2 f_n''\), that is zf, zd, zs followed by the degree character (zf0, zd0, zs0 for \(n = 0\), zf2, … ; §5.3).

docs.title: 3.5 Selection rules
docs.text:
• The angular factors of (2.7) are \(P_n\), \(xP_n\), \(\sin\theta P_n\) and \(\sin^2\theta\thinspace P_n'\), polynomials in \(x\) (up to the \(\sin\theta\) factors absorbed by \(\partial_\theta Y\) and \(Z\)) of degree at most \(n + 1\). So \(W\) from degree \(l\) reaches the target degrees \(\lvert l' - l\rvert \le n + 1\).
  • \(\Delta\Omega\) is even in \(x\), so \(\mathbf W\) keeps the equatorial symmetry of \(\mathbf u\). In kore's ordering the poloidal and toroidal degrees of one symmetry class alternate, so same-type couplings (\(P \to P\), \(T \to T\)) have even \(\Delta l\) and mixed ones (\(P \leftrightarrow T\)) odd \(\Delta l\).
  • Together: \(\lvert\Delta l\rvert \le n\) for \(P \to P\) and \(T \to T\), and \(\le n + 1\) for \(P \leftrightarrow T\) (diff_rot.max_dl, line 425). For \(\Delta\Omega = f_0 + f_2P_2\): \(\Delta l \in \lbrace 0, \pm 2\rbrace\) and \(\lbrace\pm 1, \pm 3\rbrace\); the \(f_0\) terms alone have \(\Delta l = 0\) and \(\pm 1\), like the Coriolis force.
  • For \(m = 0\) the Doppler term vanishes, but the Coriolis and shear terms do not.

The coupled problem is therefore wider than with uniform rotation: the row block of degree \(l'\) has entries in the column blocks of up to \(n_{\max} + 1\) neighbouring degrees of each type.

docs.title: 3.6 Closed forms for \(P_0\) and \(P_2\)
docs.text:
For \(n = 0\) and \(n = 2\) the coefficients of the table of §3.4 were first derived in closed form. kore now builds every degree with the algebra of §3.3, and the closed forms are kept as its validation in tests/diff_rot/diff_rot_coefficients.py (44 functions, \(\lvert\Delta l\rvert \le 3\), and the \(\sigma_n\) of (2.10)): f_* and df_*, d2f_* for \(f_2\) (\(P_2\), unnormalised, despite "Y20" in the comments), f0_*, df0_*, d2f0_* for \(f_0\). Each function takes the target degree l, m and offdiag = \(l - l'\) (source minus target) and returns the coefficient, already multiplied by \(L'\), with explicit conditions where a degree would fall below \(m\) or below 1.

Two worked examples show the structure.

  • \(T \to T\), \(P_0\), \(\Delta l = 0\). With \(P_n = 1\), the T entries of the table of §3.3 give \(C^t_T = \left[i m L n_l + 2\int x(\partial_\theta Y Z^\ast - Z\partial_\theta Y^\ast)d\Omega\right]/(L n_l)\). For real \(Y\) and \(\partial_\theta Y\) the integral is \(-2im\int x Y\partial_\theta Y\thinspace d\theta\thinspace d\phi = -i m n_l\), so \(L C^t_T = i m (L - 2)\), which is f0_1C_D0T = 1j*(-2 + l + l**2)*m. The \(i m L\) is the Doppler term, and \(-2im\) is the local Coriolis force: compare operators.coriolis, whose \(T \to T\) row is \(-2 i m G\thinspace v_1/L^3\).
  • \(P \to T\), \(P_0\), \(\Delta l = -1\). For constant \(f_0 = a\), f0_1C_D0P = \(2(l-1)^2(l+1)\sqrt{l^2 - m^2}/(2l - 1)\) and f0_1C_lho1_D0P = f0_1C_D1P = \(-2(l^2 - 1)\sqrt{l^2 - m^2}/(2l - 1)\) are \(2L\) times the coefficients \(C(l - 1)\) and \(-C\) of the \(\Delta l = -1\) Coriolis row, \(C = (l-1)\sqrt{l^2 - m^2}/(l(2l - 1))\) (operators.coriolis, line 90). So a uniform \(f_0 = a\) gives exactly \(a\) times the Coriolis operator plus \(i m G a\) times the inertia operator, which is (2.12) at the matrix level.

The algebra (§3.3) and the closed forms agree to round-off, \(\le 1.3\times 10^{-15}\) of the largest coefficient of the same row block, up to lmax 1025 (tests/diff_rot/gen_check.py, §9). Entry by entry, the closed forms are the more accurate: a few coefficients are small differences of terms of size \(O(L)\) in the algebra of §3.4 (for example df0_2C_D1P = \(2im\) exactly, \(-L(C^s_a + L_l C^s_{dq})\) in the algebra), so their own relative error grows like \(L\epsilon\), about \(10^{-10}\) at \(l \approx 1000\), while staying at round-off on the scale of the row, which is the scale at which they enter \(A\). Moving the profile \(f\) through the curls analytically before projecting would remove these cancellations; it has not been needed.

docs.title: 3.7 The heat-equation terms in harmonic form
docs.text:
Multiplication by a function of \(x\) is a matrix on the degree index. With Schmidt harmonics and \(p_l = \sqrt{(l+1)^2 - m^2}/(2l+1)\), \(q_l = \sqrt{l^2 - m^2}/(2l+1)\):

\[ x\thinspace Y_l = p_l Y_{l+1} + q_l Y_{l-1} \quad\to X, \qquad (1 - x^2)\frac{dY_l}{dx} = (l+1)q_l Y_{l-1} - l p_l Y_{l+1} \quad\to D , \qquad (3.8) \]

with rows the target degree and columns the source degree. Multiplying by \(P_n(x)\) is then the matrix \(P_n(X)\), and by \(P_n'(x)\) the matrix \(P_n'(X)\). These are the matrices of the angular algebra of §3.3 (angular.Algebra), shared by the momentum and heat terms.

For one source degree, \(\partial_\theta S_{tw} = -\sin\theta\sum_n\sigma_n P_n'(x)\), and \(\sin\theta\thinspace \partial_\theta Y = -(1 - x^2)\thinspace dY/dx = -DY\). With (3.2), the three terms of (2.11) projected on degree \(l'\) are, before the row weight and the \(p_0\) factor,

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{(a)}\quad & i m G\sum_n f_n\thinspace \left[P_n(X)\right]_ {l'l}\thinspace s_l ,\cr \text{(b)}\quad & \frac{L_l P_l}{r}\sum_n\sigma_n'\thinspace \left[P_n(X)\right]_ {l'l} ,\cr \text{(c)}\quad & \frac{a_l}{r}\sum_n\sigma_n\thinspace \left[P_n'(X)\thinspace D\right]_ {l'l} ,\cr \text{(c}')\quad & -\frac{i m T_l}{r}\sum_n\sigma_n\thinspace \left[P_n'(X)\right]_ {l'l} . \end{aligned} \qquad (3.9) \]

(c) and (c′) are the poloidal and toroidal parts of the latitudinal term. The couplings are \(\Delta l \in \lbrace 0, \pm 2, \dots, \pm n_{\max}\rbrace\) for (a) (\(s \to s\)), \(\lbrace 0, \pm 2, \dots, \pm n_{tw}\rbrace\) for (b), (c) (\(P \to s\)) and \(\lbrace\pm 1, \dots, \pm(n_{tw} - 1)\rbrace\) for (c′) (\(T \to s\)), with \(n_{tw}\) the highest degree of \(S_{tw}\) (diff_rot.tw_nmax).

docs.title: 4. Implementation overview
docs.text:
Everything specific to the differential rotation is in one module, bin/diff_rot.py, built on the angular algebra of bin/angular.py. The rest of kore calls it:

stage what it does for the differential rotation where parameters switches, profile choice, amplitude, 'user' profiles params_default.py, lines 133–189 angular algebra \(X\), \(D\), \(P_n(X)\), the vector operations, harmonics on a grid angular.py everything else profiles, thermal wind, angular couplings, labels, blocks, Δl ranges diff_rot.py, sections 1–4 of the module radial matrices builds the .mtx of the labels it is given submatrices.py (dr.labels()), radial_profiles.burrito (dr.profile_functions()) operators thin wrappers operators.differential_rotation, thermal_diffrot assembly places the blocks, over the Δl of dr.dl_range assemble.py, lines 262–461 diagnostics powers and budgets on an \((r, \theta)\) grid, independently of the algebra utils4pp.diff_rot_setup, spin_doctor.py

diff_rot.py imports only parameters and angular at the top; utils and radial_profiles are imported inside the functions that need them. radial_profiles.burrito imports diff_rot when it meets a differential-rotation profile code, so there is no import cycle, and the angular part (_primitives, momentum_coefficients) can be imported and tested without a run directory.
